name: Improper Authentication
title: CWE-287: Improper Authentication
ai_text: In AI software, improper authentication shows up across agent frameworks, MCP servers, LLM gateways and chat front ends. The CVEs show attackers reaching these systems through ordinary network requests, login forms, WebSocket connections and API headers, then simply claiming an identity the product never verifies. In Flowise, a caller can log in as any user by naming their email, and in Langflow a remote attacker can run flows without logging in at all. MCP servers are hit too, including MCP Atlassian, Meta Ads MCP and gpt-researcher, where network callers act as the operator, use stored tokens or run code. LiteLLM and Open WebUI show the same pattern, letting forged credentials or tokens pass as valid.
description: When an actor claims to have a given identity, the product does not prove or insufficiently proves that the claim is correct.

mitigations.description: Use an authentication framework or library such as the OWASP ESAPI Authentication feature.

consequences.note: This weakness can lead to the exposure of resources or functionality to unintended actors, possibly providing attackers with sensitive information or even execute arbitrary code.

alternate_terms.description: An alternate term is authentification, which appears to be most commonly used by people from non-English-speaking countries.

AuthN is typically used as an abbreviation of authentication within the web application security community. It is also distinct from AuthZ, which is an abbreviation of authorization. The use of Auth as an abbreviation is discouraged, since it could be used for either authentication or authorization.
AuthC is used as an abbreviation of authentication, but it appears to used less frequently than AuthN.
